extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of literary criticism and creative writers interested in archetypal/structural theory
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing and producing literature by identifying archetypal structures, modes (mythic/romantic/realistic), and recurrent symbolic imagery (apocalyptic/demonic), and using these as criteria for interpretation and composition. Emphasis on 'standing back' to detect structural patterns and the devices (e.g., displacement, portents) that mediate mythic material in realistic contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and form (representation vs structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The complementary aspects of art often called 'content' (what a work represents) and 'form' (the organizing structural patterns and conventions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works both for their representational lifelikeness and for their internal structural design; examples: painting's perspective vs pictorial conventions, music's forms. Anti-pattern: treating form as external to the work (claiming formal cause lies outside the picture) which 'would destroy the whole art.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural principles analogous to musical elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary expression has grammatical rudiments analogous to musical tonality, rhythm, canonical imitation, and key conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for equivalents of tonality (dominant imagery systems), rhythm (simple/compound rhythm of language), and recurring 'keys' or centres in a body of literature; a handbook approach can isolate these rudiments for interpretation and teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of fiction (mythical → romantic → low mimetic/ironic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictional modes range from the mythical (most abstract, characters with maximum power) through romantic (displaced myth toward human experience) to low mimetic or 'realistic' modes (emphasis on plausibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify a work by where it lies on this scale: mythical = high stylization and conventionalization; romantic = suggestive mythical patterns in more human contexts; low mimetic = emphasis on verisimilitude. Example: myth→romance→realism continuum explains differences among Hawthorne, Poe, and modern realistic novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth as implicit metaphorical identity vs realism as implicit simile
rubrics_metrics.description: Myth functions as an art of implicit metaphorical identity (things are identified metaphorically: sun-god = sun), whereas realism operates as an art of implicit simile (things are comparable to life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading or composing, test whether images assert identity (mythic/metaphoric) or comparison (realistic/simile). Example: the hyphenated 'sun-god' as literal metaphor; anti-pattern: misreading overtly mythical identifications as mere realistic description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement (devices linking myth to plausibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques (analogy, significant association, incidental imagery, simile) used to 'displace' myth so it will be plausible in romance or realistic contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how successfully a work translates mythic identity into plausible human terms: good displacement uses meaningful associations (e.g., person associated with sun/trees) rather than forcing caricature. Examples: dragon-king/old king correspondences; Hawthorne's statue-dove associations; failure: crude literalization that breaks plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of stylization / abstraction as indicator of mythical mode
rubrics_metrics.description: High stylization and abstract character-drawing indicate a work operating in a mythical or romantic mode rather than low mimetic realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for features like halos, statues-as-people, or unexamined supernatural devices as signs of deliberate abstraction; examples: medieval saint halos, Hawthorne's Donatello-as-statue, Poe's radical abstraction in Ligeia. Anti-pattern: criticizing such stylization solely for 'lifelikeness' ignores its mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three organizations of myth (undisplaced, romantic, realistic tendency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye's tripartite organization: (1) undisplaced myth (apocalyptic/demonic), (2) romantic tendency (implicit mythic patterns in human settings), (3) tendency of realism (emphasis on representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which organizational type predominates and how the work shifts among them; each organization carries different expectations for character power, plausibility, and symbolism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apocalyptic imagery (undisplaced positive/mythic world)
rubrics_metrics.description: A pattern of archetypal identifications centered on the city, garden, and sheepfold, and their equivalents (One God = one Man = One Lamb = One Tree = One Building), with associated imagery of light, fire, ascent, and sacramental identifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating imagery, map occurrences to apocalyptic categories: city = temple/building, garden = tree/vegetation, sheepfold = domesticated animal imagery; note transpositions (Christ as unity across categories), Trinity implications, and features like burning/golden city, ascending light, and sacramental food–wine symbolism. Examples: Biblical Apocalypse as grammar for apocalyptic imagery; alchemical correspondences (gold, jewel, elixir).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonic imagery (undisplaced negative/mythic world)
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposite of apocalyptic: nightmare, scapegoat, ruins, instruments of torture, parody of heaven; presents world as hostile, inscrutable fate administered by remote gods and parodying divine abundance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect images of bondage, catacombs, parody-religious symbols, ruins, and menacing natural powers; evaluate whether such demonic patterns function as thematic counterpoints to apocalyptic or as existential worldviews (e.g., modern dystopias like 1984).

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetypal metaphor / concrete universal
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle that a concrete universal (archetypal metaphor) identifies one category with others (e.g., city/garden/sheepfold with divine/human/animal), enabling cross-level symbolism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess uses of identifying metaphors (transubstantiation, totemic identifications, 'one body' political metaphors); examine theological or cultural conventions (Trinity, sacramental imagery) as literary devices, not merely theological claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagogic versus archetypal levels (positioning of elements like fire/water)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction where on the archetypal/anagogic scale elements occupy higher or lower places (fire above human life associated with spiritual realm; water below associated with chaos/death), and human constructions may invert or contain nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read imagery spatially/topically: fire/light as ascending/spiritual, water/depth as below/death/chaos; evaluate how a text positions trials (ordeals of water and fire) or depicts the 'way' (roads, ladders) in quest narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of portents, omens, and prophecy as structural devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Portents and prophecies are literary devices that give beginning–end symmetry and imply an ineluctable structure, though the only ineluctable will may be the author's design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether such devices serve thematic purpose (fate vs authorial design), create formal symmetry, or function as 'trompe l'oeil' illusions; examples: Anna Karenina's death omen, Sophoclean portents adapted to dramatic structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Standing back': critical distances for analysis (rhetorical → content → archetypal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different critical distances reveal different features: close (rhetorical/new criticism) shows diction and detail; intermediate reveals represented content; great distance reveals archetypal organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt appropriate critical distance for the question: fine-grained rhetorical analysis vs mid-level reading for lifelikeness vs far-level archetypal mapping. Examples: close study of brushwork ≈ rhetorical analysis; distant view of Madonna reveals Madonna archetype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic narratives (mythoi) as structures of imagery in movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Mythoi are the generic narrative patterns that enact archetypal structures (imagery in movement), e.g., cycles of death/revival, quest structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the underlying mythos (e.g., fertility/death–revival, quest, dragon-slayer) governing plot movement; evaluate how imagery supports the narrative type and whether displacement or stylization alters the mythos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death and revival archetype
rubrics_metrics.description: A recurrent archaic pattern where a heroine or land dies/declines and is revived (Proserpine, fertility gods, Shakespearean recoveries), manifesting across modes with varying displacement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot narrative beats of disappearance, apparent death, symbolic graves or statues, and eventual revival; ask how plausibility is managed (romance displacement vs mythic straightforwardness). Examples: Proserpine, Hermione/Perdita, Spenser's Florimell, Hawthorne's Marble Faun, Poe's Ligeia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal/vegetable/mineral identifications and pastoral/topical archetypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of animals/plants/stones as unified symbols (pastoral, totemic, sacramental) — e.g., sheep = pastoral/flock, tree/rose/lotus = vegetal archetypes, city/stone = mineral archetype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map recurrent animal/plant/stone images to broader social or theological meanings (sheepfold/pastoral, rose in Western apocalyptic, lotus in Eastern contexts); watch for culturally variable substitutes (horse in Upanishads vs lamb in Christian symbolism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Romantic fixation and devices of stylized association
rubrics_metrics.description: Romantic tendency to suggest implicit mythic patterns through significant association rather than literal identity, often used by ascendant classes or to idealize content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how romance uses symbolism to idealize or conventionalize experience (figures associated with doves, towers, etc.), and whether such idealization functions as allegory, romance, or social expression. Anti-pattern: wrongly applying low-mimetic expectations to romantic stylization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire: phases, techniques, and their archetypal functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire operates through parody, reversal, digressive self-parody, invective, and phases that move from conservative mockery of giants to high verbal exuberance and finally ironic/tragic perspectives; it functions to break up stereotypes and prevent domination of conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing satiric works, note phase (first: giant-killer/ironic reversal; second: analytic reductio ad absurdum; third: torrential invective and cataloguing; later phases move toward ironic/tragic distance), devices (danse macabre, kataplous, digressiveness, mock-oracular conclusions). Examples: Lucian, Rabelais, Tristram Shandy, Swift, Joyce. Consider how satire reconfigures archetypal material (e.g., other-world as ironic counterpart).
